chapters.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter XVII
paragraphs: Natasha was calmer but no happier. She didn't just avoid all outward forms of pleasure—balls, walks, concerts, and theaters—she never laughed without a trace of tears in her laughter. She couldn't sing. As soon as she started to laugh or tried to sing by herself, tears would choke her: tears of remorse, tears at the memory of those pure times that could never come back, tears of frustration that she had so uselessly ruined her young life, which might have been so happy. Laughing and singing especially felt like blasphemy in the face of her grief. Without needing any self-restraint, no desire to flirt ever entered her mind. She said and felt at that time that no man meant more to her than Nastasya Ivanovna, the household clown. Something stood guard inside her and forbade every joy. Besides, she had lost all the old interests of her carefree girlish life that had been so full of hope. The previous autumn—the hunting, "Uncle," and the Christmas holidays spent with Nicholas at Otradnoe—were what she recalled most often and most painfully. What wouldn't she have given to bring back even a single day of that time! But it was gone forever. Her feeling at the time had not deceived her—that state of freedom and readiness for any enjoyment would never return. Yet she had to go on living.

It comforted her to think that she was not better, as she had once imagined, but worse—much worse—than anybody else in the world. But this wasn't enough. She knew it, and asked herself, "What's next?" But there was nothing to come. There was no joy in life, yet life was passing. Natasha apparently tried not to be a burden or a hindrance to anyone, but wanted nothing for herself. She kept away from everyone in the house and felt at ease only with her brother Petya. She liked being with him better than with anyone else, and when alone with him she sometimes laughed. She hardly ever left the house, and of those who came to visit she was glad to see only one person—Pierre. It would have been impossible to treat her with more gentleness, greater care, and at the same time more seriousness than Count Bezukhov did. Natasha unconsciously felt this gentleness and so found great pleasure in his company. But she wasn't even grateful to him for it; nothing good on Pierre's part seemed like an effort—it seemed so natural for him to be kind to everyone that there was no merit in his kindness. Sometimes Natasha noticed embarrassment and awkwardness in him when he was around her, especially when he wanted to do something to please her or feared that something they were talking about would awaken painful memories. She noticed this and attributed it to his general kindness and shyness, which she imagined was the same toward everyone. After those involuntary words—that if he were free he would have asked on his knees for her hand and her love—spoken at a moment when she was so deeply shaken, Pierre never spoke to Natasha of his feelings; and it seemed obvious to her that those words, which had comforted her so much at the time, were spoken the way all sorts of meaningless things are said to comfort a crying child. It was not because Pierre was a married man, but because Natasha felt so strongly with him that moral barrier—the very barrier whose absence she had experienced with Kuragin—that it never entered her head that the relationship between them could lead to love on her part, still less on his, or even to the kind of tender, self-conscious, romantic friendship between a man and a woman of which she had known several examples.

Before the end of the fast of Saint Peter, Agrafena Ivanovna Belova, a country neighbor of the Rostovs, came to Moscow to pay her devotions at the shrines of the Moscow saints. She suggested that Natasha should fast and prepare for Holy Communion, and Natasha gladly welcomed the idea. Despite the doctor's orders that she should not go out early in the morning, Natasha insisted on fasting and preparing for the sacrament—not as they usually did in the Rostov family, by attending three services in their own house, but as Agrafena Ivanovna did, by going to church every day for a week and never missing Vespers, Matins, or Mass.

The countess was pleased with Natasha's devotion; after the poor results of the medical treatment, deep down she hoped that prayer might help her daughter more than medicine, and though not without fear and hiding it from the doctor, she agreed to Natasha's wish and entrusted her to Belova. Agrafena Ivanovna would come to wake Natasha at three in the morning, but generally found her already awake. She was afraid of being late for Matins. Hastily washing and humbly putting on her shabbiest dress and an old shawl, Natasha, shivering in the fresh air, went out into the deserted streets lit by the clear light of dawn. On Agrafena Ivanovna's advice, Natasha prepared herself not at their own parish church but at one where, according to the devout Agrafena Ivanovna, the priest was a man of very strict and lofty life. There were never many people in the church; Natasha always stood beside Belova in their customary place before an icon of the Blessed Virgin set into the screen before the choir on the left side, and a feeling new to her—of humility before something great and incomprehensible—seized her when, at that unusual morning hour, gazing at the dark face of the Virgin illuminated by the candles burning before it and by the morning light from the window, she listened to the words of the service and tried to follow them with understanding. When she understood them, her personal feelings became interwoven with the prayers in subtle ways of their own. When she did not understand, it was sweeter still to think that the desire to understand everything is pride, that it is impossible to understand all, that one only needs to believe and to surrender oneself to God, whom she felt guiding her soul in those moments. She crossed herself, bowed low, and when she didn't understand, in horror at her own sinfulness, simply asked God to forgive her for everything, everything, to have mercy on her. The prayers she surrendered to most fully were those of repentance. On her way home in the early hours, when she met no one but bricklayers going to work or men sweeping the street, and everybody in the houses was still asleep, Natasha experienced a new feeling—a sense of the possibility of correcting her faults, the possibility of a new, clean life, and of happiness.

Throughout the whole week she spent this way, that feeling grew every day. And the happiness of taking communion, or "communing" as Agrafena Ivanovna joyfully played with the word, seemed to Natasha so great that she felt she would never live to see that blessed Sunday.

But the happy day came, and on that memorable Sunday, when, dressed in white muslin, she returned home after communion, for the first time in many months she felt calm and no longer oppressed by the thought of the life that lay before her.
The doctor who came to see her that day ordered her to continue the powders he had prescribed two weeks earlier.
"She absolutely must keep taking them morning and evening," he said, clearly quite satisfied with his success. "Just be particular about it."

"Rest easy," he continued cheerfully, as he deftly slipped the gold coin into his palm. "She'll soon be singing and bouncing around. The last medicine has done her a world of good. She's freshened up wonderfully."
The countess, with a cheerful expression, looked down at her nails and gave a little spit for luck as she returned to the drawing room.

chapters.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter XVIII
paragraphs: At the beginning of July, increasingly alarming reports about the war began to spread through Moscow; people spoke of an appeal by the Emperor to the people and of his coming in person from the army to Moscow. And since by the eleventh of July no manifesto or appeal had been received, exaggerated reports started circulating about them and about Russia's situation. It was said that the Emperor was leaving the army because it was in danger; it was said that Smolensk had surrendered, that Napoleon had an army of a million, and that only a miracle could save Russia.

On the eleventh of July, which was a Saturday, the manifesto was received but had not yet been printed, and Pierre, who was visiting the Rostovs, promised to come to dinner the next day, Sunday, and bring a copy of the manifesto and appeal, which he would get from Count Rostopchin.

That Sunday the Rostovs went to Mass at the Razumovskis' private chapel as usual. It was a hot July day. Even at ten o'clock, when the Rostovs got out of their carriage at the chapel, the sultry air, the shouts of street vendors, the light and cheerful summer clothes of the crowd, the dusty leaves of the trees on the boulevard, the sounds of the band and the white trousers of a battalion marching to parade, the rattling of wheels on the cobblestones, and the brilliant, hot sunshine were all full of that summer languor, that mix of contentment and discontent with the present, that is felt most strongly on a bright, hot day in town. All the Moscow elite, all the Rostovs' acquaintances, were at the Razumovskis' chapel, for as if expecting something to happen, many wealthy families who usually left town for their country estates had not gone away that summer. As Natasha, at her mother's side, passed through the crowd behind a liveried footman who cleared the way for them, she heard a young man speaking about her in too loud a whisper.
"That's Rostova, the one who..."
"She's much thinner, but still pretty!"

She heard, or thought she heard, the names Kuragin and Bolkonsky. But she was always imagining that. It always seemed to her that everyone who looked at her was thinking only of what had happened to her. With a sinking heart, miserable as she always was now in a crowd, Natasha in her lilac silk dress trimmed with black lace walked—as women can—with all the more poise and dignity the greater the pain and shame in her soul. She knew for certain that she was pretty, but this no longer gave her satisfaction as it used to. On the contrary, it tormented her more than anything lately, especially on this bright, hot summer day in town. "It's Sunday again—another week gone," she thought, remembering that she had been here the Sunday before, "and always the same life that is no life, and the same surroundings in which it used to be so easy to live. I'm pretty, I'm young, and I know that now I am good. I used to be bad, but now I know I am good," she thought, "and yet my best years are slipping by and are no good to anyone." She stood by her mother's side and exchanged nods with acquaintances nearby. Out of habit she sized up the ladies' dresses, criticized the posture of a woman standing close by who wasn't crossing herself properly but in a cramped way, and again she thought with annoyance that she herself was being judged and was judging others, and suddenly, at the sound of the service, she felt horrified at her own sinfulness, horrified that the former purity of her soul was once again lost.

A handsome, fresh-looking old man was conducting the service with that gentle solemnity which has such an uplifting and soothing effect on worshipers' souls. The gates of the sanctuary screen were closed, the curtain was slowly drawn, and from behind it a soft, mysterious voice spoke certain words. Tears, the cause of which she herself did not understand, made Natasha's chest heave, and a joyous but overwhelming feeling stirred within her.
"Teach me what I should do, how to live my life, how I may become good forever, forever!" she pleaded.

The deacon came out onto the raised space before the altar screen and, holding his thumb extended, drew his long hair from under his vestment and, making the sign of the cross on his chest, began in a loud and solemn voice to recite the words of the prayer...
"In peace let us pray unto the Lord."
"As one community, without distinction of class, without enmity, united by brotherly love—let us pray!" thought Natasha.
"For the peace that is from above, and for the salvation of our souls."
"For the world of angels and all the spirits who dwell above us," prayed Natasha.

When they prayed for the warriors, she thought of her brother and Denisov. When they prayed for all traveling by land and sea, she remembered Prince Andrew, prayed for him, and asked God to forgive her all the wrongs she had done him. When they prayed for those who love us, she prayed for the members of her own family—her father and mother and Sonya—realizing for the first time how wrongly she had treated them, and feeling the full strength of her love for them. When they prayed for those who hate us, she tried to think of her enemies and people who hated her, in order to pray for them. She included among her enemies the creditors and all who had business dealings with her father, and always at the thought of enemies and those who hated her she remembered Anatole, who had done her so much harm—and though he did not hate her, she gladly prayed for him as for an enemy. Only in prayer could she think clearly and calmly of Prince Andrew and Anatole, as men for whom her feelings were as nothing compared with her awe and devotion to God. When they prayed for the Imperial family and the Synod, she bowed very low and crossed herself, saying to herself that even if she didn't understand, she could at least not doubt, and in any case she loved the governing Synod and prayed for it.
When the deacon had finished the Litany, he crossed the stole over his chest and said, "Let us commit ourselves and our whole lives to Christ the Lord!"

"Commit ourselves to God," Natasha inwardly repeated. "Lord God, I surrender myself to Your will!" she thought. "I want nothing, wish for nothing; teach me what to do and how to use my will! Take me, take me!" prayed Natasha, with urgent emotion in her heart, not crossing herself but letting her slender arms hang down as if expecting some invisible power at any moment to seize her and deliver her from herself, from her regrets, desires, remorse, hopes, and sins.
The countess looked round several times at her daughter's softened face and shining eyes, and prayed God to help her.

Unexpectedly, in the middle of the service, and not in the usual order Natasha knew so well, the deacon brought out a small stool—the one he knelt on during Trinity Sunday prayers—and placed it before the doors of the sanctuary screen. The priest came out wearing his purple velvet cap, adjusted his hair, and knelt down with effort. Everyone followed his example and looked at one another in surprise. Then came the prayer just received from the Synod—a prayer for the deliverance of Russia from foreign invasion.
"Lord God of might, God of our salvation!" began the priest in that clear, not showy but gentle voice in which only the Slavic clergy read and which acts so powerfully on the Russian heart.

"Lord God of might, God of our salvation! Look this day in mercy and blessing on Your humble people, and graciously hear us, spare us, and have mercy upon us! This foe, laying waste Your land and desiring to devastate the whole world, rises against us; these lawless men are gathered together to overthrow Your kingdom, to destroy Your beloved Jerusalem, Your beloved Russia; to defile Your temples, to overthrow Your altars, and to desecrate our holy places. How long, O Lord, how long shall the wicked triumph? How long shall they wield unlawful power?"

"Lord God! Hear us when we pray to You; strengthen with Your might our most gracious sovereign lord, Emperor Alexander Pavlovich; remember his uprightness and meekness, reward him according to his righteousness, and let it preserve us, Your chosen Israel! Bless his counsels, his undertakings, and his work; strengthen his kingdom by Your almighty hand, and give him victory over his enemy, as You gave Moses victory over Amalek, Gideon over Midian, and David over Goliath. Preserve his army, put a bow of brass in the hands of those who have armed themselves in Your Name, and gird them with strength for the fight. Take up the spear and shield and arise to help us; confound and put to shame those who have devised evil against us, may they be before the faces of Your faithful warriors as dust before the wind, and may Your mighty Angel confound them and put them to flight; may they be trapped when they least expect it, and may the plots they have laid in secret be turned against them; let them fall before Your servants' feet and be laid low by our forces! Lord, You are able to save both great and small; You are God, and no man can prevail against You!"

"God of our fathers! Remember Your bounteous mercy and loving-kindness which are from of old; turn not Your face from us, but be gracious to our unworthiness, and in Your great goodness and Your many mercies overlook our transgressions and sins! Create in us a clean heart and renew a right spirit within us, strengthen us all in Your faith, fortify our hope, inspire us with true love one for another, arm us with unity of spirit in the righteous defense of the heritage You gave to us and to our fathers, and let not the scepter of the wicked be exalted against the destiny of those You have sanctified."

"O Lord our God, in whom we believe and in whom we put our trust, let us not be disappointed in our hope of Your mercy, and give us a sign of Your blessing, that those who hate us and our Orthodox faith may see it and be put to shame and perish, and may all the nations know that You are the Lord and we are Your people. Show Your mercy upon us this day, O Lord, and grant us Your salvation; make the hearts of Your servants rejoice in Your mercy; strike down our enemies and destroy them swiftly beneath the feet of Your faithful servants! For You are the defense, the help, and the victory of those who put their trust in You, and to You be all glory, to Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, now and forever, world without end. Amen."

In Natasha's receptive state of soul, this prayer affected her powerfully. She listened to every word about the victory of Moses over Amalek, of Gideon over Midian, and of David over Goliath, and about the destruction of "Your Jerusalem," and she prayed to God with the tenderness and emotion that overflowed from her heart, but without fully understanding what she was asking of God in that prayer. She shared with all her heart in the prayer for the spirit of righteousness, for the strengthening of the heart by faith and hope, and its kindling by love. But she could not pray that her enemies be trampled underfoot when only minutes before she had been wishing she had more of them so she could pray for them. Yet neither could she doubt the righteousness of the prayer being read on bended knees. She felt in her heart a devout and trembling awe at the thought of the punishment that falls on people for their sins, and especially her own, and she prayed to God to forgive them all, and her too, and to give them all, and her too, peace and happiness. And it seemed to her that God heard her prayer.

chapters.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter XIX
paragraphs: From the day Pierre left the Rostovs' with Natasha's grateful look fresh in his mind and gazed at the comet that seemed to hang fixed in the sky, feeling that something new was appearing on his own horizon—from that day the problem of the vanity and uselessness of all earthly things, which had tormented him constantly, no longer presented itself. That terrible question—"Why?" "What for?"—which had haunted him during every activity, was now replaced not by another question or by an answer to the old one, but by her image. When he listened to or took part in trivial conversations, when he read or heard of human baseness or folly, he was not horrified as before and did not ask himself why people struggled so over these things when everything is so fleeting and incomprehensible—instead he remembered her as he had last seen her, and all his doubts vanished. Not because she had answered the questions that haunted him, but because the thought of her instantly transported him to another, brighter realm of spiritual life in which no one could be justified or guilty—a realm of beauty and love that was worth living for. Whatever worldly baseness confronted him, he said to himself:

"So what if so-and-so has cheated the country and the Tsar, and the country and the Tsar shower him with honors—what does that matter? She smiled at me yesterday and asked me to come again, and I love her, and no one will ever know it." And his soul felt calm and at peace.

Pierre still went into society, drank as much, and led the same idle and aimless life, because besides the hours he spent at the Rostovs' there were other hours he had to fill somehow, and the habits and acquaintances he had made in Moscow formed a current that carried him along irresistibly. But lately, as more and more disturbing reports came from the war front and Natasha's health began to improve—so that she no longer aroused in him that former feeling of tender pity—an ever-growing restlessness that he couldn't explain took hold of him. He felt that his present situation couldn't continue much longer, that a catastrophe was coming that would change his whole life, and he impatiently looked everywhere for signs of that approaching catastrophe. One of his brother Masons had revealed to Pierre the following prophecy concerning Napoleon, drawn from the Revelation of Saint John.
In chapter 13, verse 18, of the Apocalypse, it says:
Here is wisdom. Let him that has understanding count the number of the beast: for it is the number of a man; and his number is six hundred sixty-six.
And in the fifth verse of the same chapter:
And there was given unto him a mouth speaking great things and blasphemies; and power was given unto him to continue forty and two months.
The French alphabet, written out with the same numerical values as the Hebrew—where the first nine letters represent units and the rest represent tens—yields the following values:

Writing the words L'Empereur Napoleon in numbers, the sum comes to 666, and Napoleon was therefore the beast foretold in the Apocalypse. Moreover, by applying the same system to the words quarante-deux (forty-two), which was the term allotted to the beast that "spoke great things and blasphemies," the same number 666 was obtained; from which it followed that the limit set on Napoleon's power had come in the year 1812, when the French emperor turned forty-two. This prophecy delighted Pierre, and he often asked himself what would put an end to the power of the beast—that is, Napoleon—and tried using the same letter-to-number system to find an answer to the question that consumed him. He wrote down L'Empereur Alexandre, La nation russe and added up their numbers, but the sums were either more or less than 666. Once, while doing these calculations, he wrote down his own name in French—Comte Pierre Besouhoff—but the sum didn't come out right. Then he changed the spelling, substituting a z for the s and adding de and the article le, still without getting the desired result. Then it occurred to him: if the answer to the question were contained in his name, his nationality would also be given in the answer. So he wrote Le russe Besuhof and adding up the numbers got 671. This was only five too much, and five was represented by e, the very letter dropped from the article le before the word Empereur. By leaving out that e—though incorrectly—Pierre got the answer he sought. L'russe Besuhof made 666. This discovery excited him. How, or by what means, he was connected with the great event foretold in the Apocalypse he didn't know, but he didn't doubt that connection for a moment. His love for Natasha, the Antichrist, Napoleon, the invasion, the comet, 666, L'Empereur Napoleon, and L'russe Besuhof—all of this had to ripen and come together, to lift him out of that bewitched, petty sphere of Moscow habits in which he felt trapped, and lead him to a great achievement and great happiness.
* Forty-two.

On the eve of the Sunday when the special prayer was to be read, Pierre had promised the Rostovs to bring them both the appeal to the people and the latest army news from Count Rostopchin, whom he knew well. That morning, when he went to call on Rostopchin, he ran into a courier fresh from the army, someone he knew, who often danced at Moscow balls.
"Please, for heaven's sake, take some of this off my hands!" said the courier. "I've got a whole sackful of letters to parents."

Among these letters was one from Nicholas Rostov to his father. Pierre took it, and Rostopchin also gave him the Emperor's appeal to Moscow—just printed—the latest army orders, and his own most recent bulletin. Scanning the army orders, Pierre found in one of them, in the lists of killed, wounded, and decorated, the name of Nicholas Rostov, awarded a Saint George's Cross of the Fourth Class for courage shown in the Ostrovnoe engagement, and in the same dispatch the name of Prince Andrew Bolkonsky, appointed to command a regiment of light infantry. Though he didn't want to remind the Rostovs of Bolkonsky, Pierre couldn't resist making them happy with the news of their son's decoration, so he sent the printed army order and Nicholas's letter to the Rostovs, keeping the appeal, the bulletin, and the other orders to bring with him to dinner.

His conversation with Count Rostopchin and the latter's tone of anxious haste, the meeting with the courier who spoke casually about how badly things were going in the army, the rumors about the discovery of spies in Moscow and about a leaflet circulating in which Napoleon promised to be in both Russian capitals by autumn, and the talk of the Emperor's expected arrival the next day—all of this freshly stirred the feeling of agitation and expectation that Pierre had been conscious of ever since the appearance of the comet, and especially since the beginning of the war.

He had long been thinking of joining the army and would have done so had he not been held back, first, by his membership in the Society of Freemasons, to which he was bound by oath and which preached perpetual peace and the abolition of war, and secondly, by the fact that when he saw the great mass of Muscovites donning uniforms and talking patriotism, he somehow felt embarrassed to take the step. But the main reason for not carrying out his intention lay in the vague idea that he was L'russe Besuhof, who bore the number of the beast, 666; that his part in the great task of setting a limit to the power of the beast that spoke great and blasphemous things had been predestined from eternity, and that therefore he ought not to undertake anything, but simply wait for what was bound to come.

chapters.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter XX
paragraphs: A few close friends were dining with the Rostovs that day, as usual on Sundays.
Pierre came early so as to find them alone.
He had grown so stout that year that he would have looked abnormal had he not been so tall, so broad-limbed, and so strong that he carried his bulk with obvious ease.

He climbed the stairs, puffing and muttering something. His coachman didn't even ask whether to wait. He knew that when his master was at the Rostovs' he stayed until midnight. The Rostovs' footman rushed eagerly forward to help him off with his cloak and take his hat and stick. Pierre, from his club habit, always left both hat and stick in the front hall.

The first person he saw in the house was Natasha. Even before he saw her, while taking off his cloak, he heard her. She was practicing scales in the music room. He knew she hadn't sung since her illness, and the sound of her voice surprised and delighted him. He opened the door softly and saw her in the lilac dress she had worn at church, walking around the room singing. She had her back to him when he opened the door, but when she turned quickly and saw his broad, surprised face, she blushed and hurried up to him.
"I want to try singing again," she said, adding as if by way of excuse, "it is at least something to do."
"That's wonderful!"
"How glad I am you've come! I'm so happy today," she said, with the old liveliness Pierre hadn't seen in her for a long time. "You know Nicholas got a Saint George's Cross? I'm so proud of him."
"Oh yes, I sent that announcement along. But I don't want to interrupt you," he added, and was about to go to the drawing room.
Natasha stopped him.
"Count, is it wrong of me to sing?" she said, blushing and fixing her eyes searchingly on him.
"No... Why should it be? On the contrary... But why do you ask me?"

"I don't know myself," Natasha answered quickly, "but I wouldn't want to do anything you disapproved of. I trust you completely. You don't know how important you are to me, how much you've done for me..." She spoke rapidly and didn't notice how Pierre flushed at her words. "I saw in that same army order that he—Bolkonsky"—she whispered the name quickly—"is in Russia, and back in the army. What do you think?" She was speaking hurriedly, obviously afraid her composure might fail. "Will he ever forgive me? Won't he always hold bitter feelings toward me? What do you think? What do you think?"
"I think..." Pierre replied, "that he has nothing to forgive.... If I were in his place..."

By association of ideas, Pierre was instantly carried back to the day when, trying to comfort her, he had said that if he were not himself but the best man in the world and free, he would ask on his knees for her hand and her love; and the same feeling of pity, tenderness, and love took hold of him, and the same words rose to his lips. But she didn't give him time to say them.

"Yes, you... you..." she said, uttering the word "you" with rapture. "That's different. I know no one kinder, more generous, or better than you—nobody could be! If you hadn't been there then, and now too, I don't know what would have become of me, because..."
Tears suddenly rose in her eyes. She turned away, lifted her sheet music before her face, and began singing again, pacing back and forth across the room.
Just then Petya came running in from the drawing room.

Petya was now a handsome, rosy-cheeked boy of fifteen with full red lips who looked like Natasha. He was preparing for the university, but he and his friend Obolensky had lately agreed, in secret, to join the hussars.
Petya had come rushing out to talk to his namesake about this plan. He had asked Pierre to find out whether he would be accepted in the hussars.
Pierre walked up and down the drawing room, not listening to what Petya was saying.
Petya pulled him by the arm to get his attention.
"Well, what about my plan? Peter Kirilych, for heaven's sake! You're my only hope," said Petya.
"Oh yes, your plan. To join the hussars? I'll mention it, I'll bring it all up today."
"Well, my dear fellow, have you got the manifesto?" asked the old count. "The countess went to Mass at the Razumovskis' and heard the new prayer. She says it's very moving."

"Yes, I've got it," said Pierre. "The Emperor is to be here tomorrow... there's to be a special meeting of the nobility, and they're talking of a levy of ten men per thousand. Oh yes, let me congratulate you!"
"Yes, yes, thank God! Well, and what's the news from the army?"
"We're retreating again. They say we're already near Smolensk," replied Pierre.
"O Lord, O Lord!" exclaimed the count. "Where's the manifesto?"
"The Emperor's appeal? Oh yes!"

Pierre started feeling in his pockets for the papers but couldn't find them. Still patting his pockets, he kissed the hand of the countess as she entered the room and glanced uneasily around, obviously expecting Natasha, who had stopped singing but hadn't yet come into the drawing room.
"I swear, I don't know what I've done with it," he said.
"There he goes, always losing everything!" remarked the countess.

Natasha came in with a softened, emotional expression on her face and sat down, looking silently at Pierre. As soon as she entered, Pierre's gloomy features suddenly brightened, and while still searching for the papers he glanced at her several times.
"No, honestly! I'll drive home—I must have left them there. I'll definitely..."
"But you'll be late for dinner."
"Oh! And my coachman has gone."
But Sonya, who had gone to look for the papers in the front hall, had found them in Pierre's hat, where he had carefully tucked them under the lining. Pierre was about to start reading.
"No, after dinner," said the old count, clearly looking forward to the reading with great anticipation.

At dinner, where champagne was drunk to the health of the new holder of the Saint George's Cross, Shinshin told them the town news: about the old Georgian princess's illness, about Metivier's disappearance from Moscow, and about how some German had been brought before Rostopchin accused of being a French "spyer" (as Count Rostopchin himself told the story), and how Rostopchin let him go, assuring the crowd that the man was "not a spy at all, but only an old German ruin."
"People are being arrested..." said the count. "I've told the countess she shouldn't speak French so much. It's not the time for it now."
"And have you heard?" Shinshin asked. "Prince Golitsyn has hired a teacher to teach him Russian. It's becoming dangerous to speak French in the streets."
"And what about you, Count Peter Kirilych? If they call up the militia, you'll have to mount a horse too," the old count remarked, turning to Pierre.
Pierre had been silent and preoccupied all through dinner, seeming not to grasp what was being said. He looked at the count.

"Oh yes, the war," he said. "No! What sort of warrior would I make? And yet everything is so strange, so strange! I can't make sense of it. I don't know—I'm very far from having military tastes—but in times like these no one can answer for himself."
After dinner the count settled himself comfortably in an easy chair and with a solemn face asked Sonya, who was considered an excellent reader, to read the appeal.
"To Moscow, our ancient Capital!"
"The enemy has entered the borders of Russia with immense forces. He comes to plunder our beloved country."
Sonya read carefully in her high-pitched voice. The count listened with closed eyes, heaving abrupt sighs at certain passages.
Natasha sat upright, gazing searchingly now at her father and now at Pierre.

Pierre felt her eyes on him and tried not to look around. The countess shook her head disapprovingly and angrily at every solemn expression in the manifesto. In all these words she saw only that the danger threatening her son would not be over soon. Shinshin, with a sarcastic smile on his lips, was clearly preparing to mock anything that gave him the opportunity: Sonya's reading, some remark of the count's, or even the manifesto itself if no better target presented itself.

After reading about the dangers threatening Russia and the hopes the Emperor placed on Moscow and especially on its distinguished nobility, Sonya, her voice quivering—mainly from the attention being paid to her—read the final words:

"We ourselves will not delay to appear among our people in that Capital and in other parts of our realm for consultation, and for the direction of all our levies, both those now barring the enemy's path and those freshly formed to defeat him wherever he may appear. May the ruin he hopes to bring upon us recoil on his own head, and may Europe, delivered from bondage, glorify the name of Russia!"

"Yes, that's it!" cried the count, opening his moist eyes and sniffing repeatedly, as if someone had held strong smelling salts under his nose; and he added, "Let the Emperor just say the word and we'll sacrifice everything and hold nothing back."
Before Shinshin had time to deliver the joke he had prepared about the count's patriotism, Natasha jumped up from her seat and ran to her father.
"What a darling our Papa is!" she cried, kissing him, and she looked at Pierre again with the unconscious flirtatiousness that had returned with her better spirits.
"There! That's a patriot for you!" said Shinshin.
"I'm not a patriot at all, I'm simply..." Natasha replied in a hurt tone. "Everything seems funny to you, but this isn't a joke at all..."
"A joke, he says!" the count put in. "Let the Emperor just say the word and we'll all go... We're not Germans!"
"But did you notice, it says 'for consultation'?" said Pierre.
"Never mind what it says..."
At this moment Petya, to whom nobody was paying any attention, came up to his father with a very flushed face and said in his breaking voice—now deep, now shrill:
"Well, Papa, I'm telling you right now—and Mama too—think what you want, but I say absolutely that you must let me join the army, because I can't... that's all."
The countess, in dismay, looked up at the ceiling, clasped her hands, and turned angrily to her husband.
"This is what comes of your talk!" she said.
But the count had already recovered from his excitement.
"Come, come!" he said. "What a fine warrior you are! No! Nonsense! You have to study."

"It's not nonsense, Papa. Fedya Obolensky is younger than me, and he's going too. Besides, I can't study now when..." Petya stopped short, blushing until he perspired, but still got out the words, "when our Fatherland is in danger."
"That's enough, that's enough—nonsense..."
"But you said yourself we'd sacrifice everything."
"Petya! Be quiet, I tell you!" cried the count, with a glance at his wife, who had turned pale and was staring fixedly at her son.
"And I'm telling you—Peter Kirilych here will tell you too..."

"Nonsense, I tell you. You've barely stopped nursing at your mother's breast and you want to go to war! There, there, enough," and the count started to leave the room with the papers, probably to reread them in his study before having a nap.
"Well, Peter Kirilych, let's go have a smoke," he said.
Pierre was agitated and confused. Natasha's unusually brilliant eyes, continually glancing at him with more than friendly warmth, had put him in this state.
"No, I think I'll go home."

"Home? Why? You were going to spend the evening with us... You don't come often enough as it is, and this girl of mine," said the count good-naturedly, nodding toward Natasha, "only brightens up when you're here."
"Yes, I forgot... I really must go home... business..." said Pierre hurriedly.
"Well then, goodbye!" said the count, and left the room.
"Why are you going? Why are you upset?" asked Natasha, and she looked challengingly into Pierre's eyes.
"Because I love you!" was what he wanted to say, but he didn't say it. He only blushed until the tears came, lowered his eyes.
"Because it's better for me to come less often... because... No, I simply have business..."
"Why? No, tell me!" Natasha began firmly, and suddenly stopped.
They looked at each other with dismayed and embarrassed faces. He tried to smile but couldn't: his smile expressed suffering, and he silently kissed her hand and went out.
Pierre made up his mind not to go to the Rostovs' anymore.

chapters.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter XXI
paragraphs: After being firmly refused, Petya went to his room, locked himself in, and wept bitterly. When he came in for tea—silent, gloomy, and with a tear-stained face—everybody pretended not to notice anything.

The next day the Emperor arrived in Moscow, and several of the Rostovs' household servants asked permission to go see him. That morning Petya spent a long time dressing and arranging his hair and collar to look like a grown-up man. He frowned at himself in the mirror, gestured, shrugged his shoulders, and finally, without a word to anyone, took his cap and left the house by the back door, trying to slip out unnoticed. Petya had decided to go straight to wherever the Emperor was and explain frankly to some gentleman-in-waiting (he imagined the Emperor was always surrounded by gentlemen-in-waiting) that he, Count Rostov, despite his youth, wished to serve his country; that youth was no barrier to loyalty, and that he was ready to... While getting dressed, Petya had prepared many fine things he meant to say to the gentleman-in-waiting.

It was precisely the fact of being so young that Petya counted on for reaching the Emperor—he even imagined how surprised everyone would be at his youthfulness—and yet in the arrangement of his collar and hair and in his measured, deliberate walk, he wanted to appear grown-up. But the farther he went and the more his attention was distracted by the ever-growing crowds heading toward the Kremlin, the less he remembered to walk with grown-up poise. As he approached the Kremlin he even began trying to avoid being crushed and stuck out his elbows menacingly. But inside the Trinity Gateway he was squeezed so hard against the wall by people who were probably unaware of his patriotic intentions that, despite all his determination, he had to give in and stop while carriages rumbled through the archway. Beside Petya stood a peasant woman, a footman, two shopkeepers, and a discharged soldier. After standing in the gateway for some time, Petya tried to push forward ahead of the others without waiting for all the carriages to pass, and he began working his way with his elbows, but the woman in front of him—the first person he tried this on—angrily shouted at him:
"What are you shoving for, young lord? Can't you see we're all standing still? So why push?"
"Anyone can shove," said the footman, and he too started using his elbows so vigorously that he shoved Petya into a very dirty corner of the gateway.
Petya wiped his sweating face with his hands and straightened the damp collar he had arranged so carefully at home to look manly.

He felt that he no longer looked presentable and feared that if he approached the gentlemen-in-waiting in this state, he wouldn't be admitted to the Emperor. But it was impossible to straighten himself up or move to another spot because of the crowd. One of the generals driving past was someone the Rostovs knew, and Petya thought of asking for his help, but decided that wouldn't be a manly thing to do. When the carriages had all passed, the crowd, carrying Petya with it, surged forward into the Kremlin Square, which was already packed with people. There were crowds not only in the square but everywhere—on the slopes and on the rooftops. As soon as Petya found himself in the square, he clearly heard the sound of bells and the joyous voices of the crowd that filled the whole Kremlin.

For a while the crowd was less dense, but suddenly all heads were bared and everyone rushed forward in one direction. Petya was being pressed so hard he could barely breathe, and everybody shouted, "Hurrah! Hurrah! Hurrah!" Petya stood on tiptoe and pushed and shoved, but could see nothing except the people around him.
Every face wore the same expression of excitement and enthusiasm. A shopkeeper's wife standing beside Petya sobbed, and tears streamed down her cheeks.
"Father! Angel! Dear one!" she kept repeating, wiping away her tears with her fingers.
"Hurrah!" was heard on all sides.
For a moment the crowd stood still, then surged forward again.

Completely beside himself, Petya, clenching his teeth and rolling his eyes fiercely, pushed forward, elbowing his way and shouting "Hurrah!" as if prepared that instant to kill himself and everyone else—but on both sides of him, other people with equally fierce faces pushed forward too, and everybody shouted "Hurrah!"

"So this is what the Emperor is!" thought Petya. "No, I can't petition him myself—that would be too bold." But despite this he continued to struggle desperately forward, and through gaps between the backs of those ahead he caught glimpses of an open space with a strip of red cloth spread over it. But just then the crowd swayed back—the police up front were pushing back those who had pressed too close to the procession; the Emperor was passing from the palace to the Cathedral of the Assumption—and Petya suddenly got such a blow to his side and ribs, and was squeezed so hard, that everything went dark before his eyes and he lost consciousness. When he came to, a man of clerical appearance with a tuft of gray hair at the back of his head, wearing a shabby blue cassock—probably a church clerk and choir singer—was holding him up by the arm with one hand while fending off the crowd with the other.
"You've crushed the young gentleman!" said the clerk. "What's wrong with you? Easy there!... They've crushed him, crushed him!"

The Emperor entered the Cathedral of the Assumption. The crowd spread out more evenly again, and the clerk led Petya—pale and breathless—to the Tsar Cannon. Several people felt sorry for Petya, and suddenly a group turned toward him and crowded around. Those nearest him tended to him, unbuttoned his coat, sat him on the raised platform of the cannon, and scolded those others (whoever they might be) who had crushed him.
"He could easily have been killed! What kind of behavior is that? Killing people! Poor boy, he's white as a sheet!" various voices were saying.

Petya soon came to himself; the color returned to his face, the pain passed, and at the cost of that temporary unpleasantness he had gained a spot by the cannon from where he hoped to see the Emperor on his way back. Petya no longer thought about presenting his petition. If he could only see the Emperor, he would be happy!

While the service went on in the Cathedral of the Assumption—a combined service of prayer for the Emperor's arrival and thanksgiving for the peace with Turkey—the crowd outside spread out, and vendors appeared selling kvass, gingerbread, and poppy-seed sweets (of which Petya was especially fond), and ordinary conversation could be heard again. A shopkeeper's wife was showing a tear in her shawl and telling how much it had cost; another was saying that all silk goods had become expensive. The clerk who had rescued Petya was chatting with a government official about the priests conducting the service that day with the bishop. The clerk kept using the word "plenary," a word Petya didn't understand. Two young townsmen were joking with some servant girls who were cracking nuts. All these conversations, especially the flirting with the girls, were the kind that would normally have fascinated Petya at his age, but they didn't interest him now. He sat on his perch—the pedestal of the cannon—still stirred by the thought of the Emperor and his love for him. The feeling of pain and fear he had experienced when he was being crushed, combined with rapture, further intensified his sense of the importance of the occasion.

Suddenly the boom of cannons was heard from the embankment, celebrating the signing of peace with Turkey, and the crowd rushed toward the embankment to watch. Petya wanted to run there too, but the clerk who had taken the young gentleman under his protection stopped him. The firing was still going on when officers, generals, and courtiers came hurrying out of the cathedral, and after them others at a more leisurely pace: caps were raised again, and those who had run to see the cannons came running back. At last four men in uniforms and sashes emerged from the cathedral doors. "Hurrah! Hurrah!" shouted the crowd again.

"Which one is he? Which?" asked Petya in a tearful voice, but no one answered—everyone was too excited. And Petya, fixing on one of those four men (whom he could barely see through the tears of joy filling his eyes), poured all his enthusiasm on him—though it turned out not to be the Emperor—frantically shouting "Hurrah!" and resolved that tomorrow, come what might, he would join the army.

The crowd ran after the Emperor, followed him to the palace, and began to disperse. It was already late and Petya hadn't eaten anything and was drenched in sweat, yet he didn't go home. He stood with the dwindling but still considerable crowd before the palace while the Emperor dined, gazing in at the palace windows, expecting he knew not what, and equally envying the dignitaries arriving at the entrance to dine with the Emperor and the court footmen serving at table, glimpses of whom could be seen through the windows.
While the Emperor was dining, Valuev, looking out the window, said:
"The people are still hoping to see Your Majesty again."
The dinner was nearly over, and the Emperor, munching a biscuit, rose and went out onto the balcony. The crowd, with Petya among them, rushed toward the balcony.
"Angel! Dear one! Hurrah! Father!" cried the crowd, and Petya with it, and again the women and the more tenderhearted men—Petya among them—wept with joy.

A largish piece of the biscuit the Emperor was holding broke off, fell onto the balcony railing, and then to the ground. A coachman in a short jacket who stood nearest sprang forward and snatched it up. Several people in the crowd rushed at the coachman. Seeing this, the Emperor had a plateful of biscuits brought to him and began throwing them down from the balcony. Petya's eyes grew bloodshot, and still more excited by the danger of being crushed, he lunged at the biscuits. He didn't know why, but he had to have a biscuit from the Tsar's hand, and he felt he must not give way. He sprang forward and knocked over an old woman who was reaching for a biscuit. The old woman didn't consider herself beaten, even though she was on the ground—she grabbed at some biscuits, but her hand couldn't reach them. Petya knocked her hand away with his knee, seized a biscuit, and as if afraid of being too late, shouted "Hurrah!" again in a voice already hoarse.
The Emperor went inside, and after that most of the crowd began to disperse.
"There! I said if we just waited—and so it was!" people were saying happily.

Happy as Petya was, he felt sad at having to go home knowing that all the excitement of the day was over. He didn't go straight home from the Kremlin but stopped by his friend Obolensky's house—Obolensky was fifteen and was also joining the regiment. When he got home, Petya announced firmly and resolutely that if he wasn't allowed to enlist, he would run away. And the next day, Count Ilya Rostov—though he hadn't entirely given in—went to find out how to arrange for Petya to serve somewhere with the least possible danger.
